title: Forms and validation
lesson: A form is how people hand your app data, and people make mistakes: a blank box, "forty" instead of 40, a stray space, 4000 kg typed as 40000. **Validation** means checking input before you trust it, and telling the person clearly how to fix it. Good validation is kind: it says what's wrong *next to the box that's wrong*, in plain words. **Two layers.** HTML can check the basics for free: ``` ``` `required` refuses an empty box, `type="number"` gives a number keypad on phones, and `min`/`max` set the range. But HTML checks aren't enough on their own: their messages can't be customised much, they don't know your rules ("this farmer isn't in the group"), and anyone can switch them off. So **always check again in JavaScript** (and a real server checks a third time). **Reading inputs, the careful way.** `.value` is *always text*, even in a number box. ``` const name = nameBox.value.trim(); // " Amina " becomes "Amina" const text = kgBox.value.trim(); const kg = Number(text); ``` The trap: `Number("")` is `0`, not an error. Check for an empty box *before* converting, or a blank field quietly becomes zero kilograms. `Number("abc")` is `NaN`; test it with `Number.isNaN(kg)` (or `Number.isFinite(kg)`, which also rejects Infinity). **Return errors, don't just print them.** Write validation as a plain function that returns an object of messages, one per bad field: ``` function validate(name, kgText) { const errors = {}; if (name.trim() === "") errors.name = "Enter the farmer's name"; if (kgText.trim() === "") errors.kg = "Enter the kg"; return errors; // {} means all good } ``` An empty object means valid: `Object.keys(errors).length === 0`. Because it's a plain function, you can test every rule without a page. **Showing errors.** Put each message in its own element beside its input, and clear old messages each time (a fixed field shouldn't keep shouting). A class like `invalid` on the input lets CSS give it a red border. `aria-describedby` links the input to its message so screen readers read the error with the field. Common mistakes: validating only in HTML; forgetting `trim()`; treating `""` as 0; showing one message at the top that doesn't say which box; and never clearing messages once fixed.

notes: Validation is a plain function returning an errors object; {} means valid.
Empty is checked before Number(), because Number("") is 0.
showErrors writes every field, so fixed fields lose their old message and red border.
The submit handler only glues them together.

exercises.title: The form page
exercises.prompt: Build the harvest form. Inside <form id="harvest-form">: a text input id="farmer" (required); a <select id="crop"> with at least 3 crops; a number input id="kg" with required, min="1" and max="5000"; an empty <span id="farmer-error"> after the farmer box and <span id="kg-error"> after the kg box; and a <button type="submit">. Every input and the select gets a <label for=...>. Link each input to its error message with aria-describedby (farmer-error, kg-error).

quiz.why: An empty string converts to 0, so check for empty boxes before converting.

quiz.q: The input has required, min and max. Why check again in JavaScript?
choices: HTML checks can be switched off, can't know your own rules, and give limited messages
quiz.why: HTML checks are a helpful first layer, not a guarantee.

quiz.q: Why return an errors object from validate() instead of setting the page's text inside it?
choices: The rules can be tested without a page, and the display can change freely

quiz.q: A person fixes the kg box but the old red message stays. What was missed?
choices: Clearing messages for fields that are now valid
quiz.why: Write every field each time, using "" for the valid ones.

quiz.q: What does aria-describedby="kg-error" on an input do?
choices: Links the input to its error message so screen readers read them together
quiz.why: Accessible forms tie each message to its field.

cards.q: Is a converted value a real number?
